[EN] Article 28 — Contracts between contracting authorities
  Act: Directive 2014/25/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on procurement by entities operating in the water, energy, transport and postal services sectors and repealing Directive 2004/17/EC (Text with EEA relevance)
  Location: CHAPTER III Material scope › Subsection 3 Special relations (cooperation, affiliated undertakings and joint ventures)
Contracts between contracting authorities

1. A contract awarded by a contracting authority to a legal person governed by private or public law shall fall outside the scope of this Directive where all of the following conditions are fulfilled:

(a)
the contracting authority exercises over the legal person concerned a control which is similar to that which it exercises over its own departments;

(b)
more than 80 % of the activities of the controlled legal person are carried out in the performance of tasks entrusted to it by the controlling contracting authority or by other legal persons controlled by that contracting authority;

(c)
there is no direct private capital participation in the controlled legal person with the exception of non-controlling and non-blocking forms of private capital participation required by national legislative provisions, in conformity with the Treaties, which do not exert a decisive influence on the controlled legal person.

A contracting authority shall be deemed to exercise over a legal person a control similar to that which it exercises over its own departments within the meaning of point (a) of the first subparagraph where it exercises a decisive influence over both strategic objectives and significant decisions of the controlled legal person. Such control may also be exercised by another legal person, which is itself controlled in the same way by the contracting authority.
2. Paragraph 1 also applies where a controlled person which is a contracting authority awards a contract to its controlling contracting authority, or to another legal person controlled by the same contracting authority, provided that there is no direct private capital participation in the legal person being awarded the public contract with the exception of non-controlling and non-blocking forms of private capital participation required by national legislative provisions, in conformity with the Treaties, which do not exert a decisive influence on the controlled legal person.

3. A contracting authority, which does not exercise over a legal person governed by private or public law control within the meaning of paragraph 1, may nevertheless award a contract to that legal person without applying this Directive, where all of the following conditions are fulfilled:

(a)
the contracting authority exercises jointly with other contracting authorities a control over that legal person which is similar to that which they exercise over their own departments;

(b)
more than 80 % of the activities of that legal person are carried out in the performance of tasks entrusted to it by the controlling contracting authorities or by other legal persons controlled by the same contracting authorities; and

(c)
there is no direct private capital participation in the controlled legal person with the exception of non-controlling and non-blocking forms of private capital participation required by national legislative provisions, in conformity with the Treaties, which do not exert a decisive influence on the controlled legal person.

For the purposes of point (a) of the first subparagraph, contracting authorities shall be deemed to exercise joint control over a legal person where all of the following conditions are fulfilled:

(i)
the decision-making bodies of the controlled legal person are composed of representatives of all participating contracting authorities. Individual representatives may represent several or all of the participating contracting authorities;

(ii)
those contracting authorities are able to jointly exert decisive influence over the strategic objectives and significant decisions of the controlled legal person; and

(iii)
the controlled legal person does not pursue any interests which are contrary to those of the controlling contracting authorities.

4. A contract concluded exclusively between two or more contracting authorities shall fall outside the scope of this Directive, where all of the following conditions are met:

(a)
the contract establishes or implements a cooperation between the participating contracting authorities with the aim of ensuring that public services they have to perform are provided with a view to achieving objectives they have in common;

(b)
the implementation of that cooperation is governed solely by considerations relating to the public interest; and

(c)
the participating contracting authorities perform on the open market less than 20 % of the activities concerned by the cooperation.

5. For the determination of the percentage of activities referred to in point (b) of the first subparagraph of paragraph 1, point (b) of the first subparagraph of paragraph 3 and point (c) of paragraph 4, the average total turnover, or an appropriate alternative activity based measure such as costs incurred by the relevant legal person with respect to services, supplies and works for the three years preceding the contract award shall be taken into consideration.Where, because of the date on which the relevant legal person was created or commenced activities or because of a reorganisation of its activities, the turnover, or alternative activity based measure such as costs, are either not available for the preceding three years or no longer relevant, it shall be sufficient to show that the measurement of activity is credible, particularly by means of business projections.

[EN] Article 13 — Conduct of Member States with regard to a bilateral investment agreement with a third country
  Act: Regulation (EU) No 1219/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2012 establishing transitional arrangements for bilateral investment agreements between Member States and third countries
  Location: CHAPTER IV FINAL PROVISIONS
Conduct of Member States with regard to a bilateral investment agreement with a third country

Where a bilateral investment agreement falls within the scope of this Regulation, the Member State concerned shall:

(a)
inform the Commission without undue delay of all meetings which will take place under the provisions of the agreement. The Commission shall be provided with the agenda and all relevant information permitting an understanding of the topics to be discussed at those meetings. The Commission may request further information from the Member State concerned. Where an issue to be discussed might affect the implementation of the Union’s policies relating to investment, including in particular the common commercial policy, the Commission may require the Member State concerned to take a particular position;

(b)
inform the Commission without undue delay of any representations made to it that a particular measure is inconsistent with the agreement. The Member State shall also immediately inform the Commission of any request for dispute settlement lodged under the auspices of the bilateral investment agreement as soon as the Member State becomes aware of such a request. The Member State and the Commission shall fully cooperate and take all necessary measures to ensure an effective defence which may include, where appropriate, the participation in the procedure by the Commission;

(c)
seek the agreement of the Commission before activating any relevant mechanisms for dispute settlement against a third country included in the bilateral investment agreement and shall, where requested by the Commission, activate such mechanisms. Those mechanisms shall include consultations with the other party to a bilateral investment agreement and dispute settlement where provided for in the agreement. The Member State and the Commission shall fully cooperate in the conduct of procedures within the relevant mechanisms, which may include, where appropriate, the participation in the relevant procedures by the Commission.

  Location: CHAPTER VII MEDICAL EXPOSURES
Optimisation

1. Member States shall ensure that all doses due to medical exposure for radiodiagnostic, interventional radiology, planning, guiding and verification purposes are kept as low as reasonably achievable consistent with obtaining the required medical information, taking into account economic and societal factors.For all medical exposure of patients for radiotherapeutic purposes, exposures of target volumes shall be individually planned and their delivery appropriately verified taking into account that doses to non-target volumes and tissues shall be as low as reasonably achievable and consistent with the intended radiotherapeutic purpose of the exposure.

2. Member States shall ensure the establishment, regular review and use of diagnostic reference levels for radiodiagnostic examinations, having regard to the recommended European diagnostic reference levels where available, and where appropriate, for interventional radiology procedures, and the availability of guidance for this purpose.

3. Member States shall ensure that for each medical or biomedical research project involving medical exposure:

(a)
the individuals concerned participate voluntarily;

(b)
these individuals are informed about the risks of exposure;

(c)
a dose constraint is established for individuals for whom no direct medical benefit is expected from exposure;

(d)
in the case of patients who voluntarily accept to undergo an experimental medical practice and who are expected to receive a diagnostic or therapeutic benefit from this practice, the dose levels concerned shall be considered on an individual basis by the practitioner and/or referrer prior to the exposure taking place.

4. Member States shall ensure that the optimisation includes the selection of equipment, the consistent production of adequate diagnostic information or therapeutic outcomes, the practical aspects of medical radiological procedures, quality assurance, and the assessment and evaluation of patient doses or the verification of administered activities, taking into account economic and societal factors.

5. Member States shall ensure that:

(a)
dose constraints are established for the exposure of carers and comforters, where appropriate;

(b)
appropriate guidance is established for the exposure of carers and comforters.

6. Member States shall ensure that in the case of a patient undergoing treatment or diagnosis with radionuclides, the practitioner or the undertaking, as specified by Member States, provides the patient or their representative with information on the risks of ionising radiation and appropriate instructions with a view to restricting doses to persons in contact with the patient as far as reasonably achievable. For therapeutic procedures these shall be written instructions.These instructions shall be handed out before leaving the hospital or clinic or a similar institution.

addresses, without giving away the legal consequence.

instrument.

messages.content:
You select the question-generation mode for an EU legislative article: "fact_pattern" or "lookup".
Choose the mode that best fits the target article’s substantive content. Do not generate questions
or answers.

INPUT STRUCTURE
The input contains four marked blocks:
- "### TARGET ARTICLE": the article that questions must be about.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES": provisions cited from the same act.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS": provisions cited from other acts.
- "### REFERENCED ANNEXES": cited annexes.

References provide context or complete the target’s rule; they must not become the subject of the
questions.

Article blocks contain a language tag, article number and title, an "Act:" line identifying the
instrument and its subject matter, and sometimes a "Location:" within the act. Other-act references
and annexes have a "Cite as:" key identifying the provision. Empty blocks are marked.
Different-language versions represent the same provision.

Use metadata to understand the legal regime, but choose based on the target article’s text.

AVAILABLE MODES

FACT_PATTERN — The practitioner knows the situation, not the governing instrument.
Questions describe a concrete case involving a private party or a national authority handling a
file. The situation includes at least two legally relevant particulars, such as the actor, activity,
product, omission, quantity, place, or time. These instantiate conditions the article explicitly
addresses, without giving away the legal consequence.

Typical information needs: whether the case is covered, permitted, prohibited, or eligible; what the
actor must do; what deadline, amount, or consequence applies. Questions do not name the governing
instrument.

LOOKUP — The practitioner knows the regime and wants one point of law.
Questions directly request a definition, scope rule, obligation, condition, deadline, threshold,
reporting requirement, consequence, competent body, or procedure. They identify the regime through a
specific actor, product, activity, or legal term, without requiring a concrete client situation.

Each question has two otherwise identical renderings: one without an instrument identifier and one
with the target instrument’s official identifier.

SELECTION
Choose fact_pattern when meaningful case particulars naturally connect a situation to the target’s
legal treatment. Choose lookup when a direct request for a legal point is more natural and adding a
case would mainly decorate the question.

Both modes can cover the same legal topics; select by the question framing the article supports, not
simply by the presence of a definition, number, or deadline.

Return "skip" when neither mode is suitable, including when the target contains only boilerplate
such as transposition, entry into force, or generic institutional review clauses.

Return valid JSON only:
{"mode": "<fact_pattern|lookup|skip>",
 "reason": "<one short sentence explaining the fit to this article>"}

  Act: Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 October 2013 laying down the Union Customs Code (recast)
  Location: CHAPTER 2 Rights and obligations of persons with regard to the customs legislation › Section 1 Provision of information
Means for the exchange and storage of information and common data requirements

1. All exchanges of information, such as declarations, applications or decisions, between customs authorities and between economic operators and customs authorities, and the storage of such information, as required under the customs legislation, shall be made using electronic data-processing techniques.

2. Common data requirements shall be drawn up for the purpose of the exchange and storage of information referred to in paragraph 1.

3. Means for the exchange and storage of information, other than the electronic data-processing techniques referred to in paragraph 1, may be used as follows:

(a)
on a permanent basis where duly justified by the type of traffic or where the use of electronic data-processing techniques is not appropriate for the customs formalities concerned;

(b)
on a temporary basis, in the event of a temporary failure of the computerised system of the customs authorities or of the economic operators.

The derogation shall be reviewed periodically and may be extended for further specific periods of time upon further application by the Member State to which it is addressed. It shall be revoked where no longer justified.The derogation shall not affect the exchange of information between the Member State to which it is addressed and other Member States nor the exchange and storage of information in other Member States for the purpose of the application of the customs legislation.

Importing and exporting Member States

3. Notification prior to arrival into ports

Subject to specific provisions on notification provided for in the applicable legal acts of the Union or under international legal instruments applicable to maritime transport and binding on the Member States, including provisions on control of persons and goods, Member States shall ensure that the master or any other person duly authorised by the operator of the ship provides notification, prior to arriving in a port situated in a Member State, of the information required under the reporting formalities to the competent authority designated by that Member State:

  Act: Directive 2014/53/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of radio equipment and repealing Directive 1999/5/EC (Text with EEA relevance)
  Location: CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS
Essential requirements

1. Radio equipment shall be constructed so as to ensure:

(a)
the protection of health and safety of persons and of domestic animals and the protection of property, including the objectives with respect to safety requirements set out in Directive 2014/35/EU, but with no voltage limit applying;

(b)
an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility as set out in Directive 2014/30/EU.

2. Radio equipment shall be so constructed that it both effectively uses and supports the efficient use of radio spectrum in order to avoid harmful interference.

3. Radio equipment within certain categories or classes shall be so constructed that it complies with the following essential requirements:

(a)
radio equipment interworks with accessories, in particular with common chargers;

(b)
radio equipment interworks via networks with other radio equipment;

(c)
radio equipment can be connected to interfaces of the appropriate type throughout the Union;

(d)
radio equipment does not harm the network or its functioning nor misuse network resources, thereby causing an unacceptable degradation of service;

(e)
radio equipment incorporates safeguards to ensure that the personal data and privacy of the user and of the subscriber are protected;

(f)
radio equipment supports certain features ensuring protection from fraud;

(g)
radio equipment supports certain features ensuring access to emergency services;

(h)
radio equipment supports certain features in order to facilitate its use by users with a disability;

(i)
radio equipment supports certain features in order to ensure that software can only be loaded into the radio equipment where the compliance of the combination of the radio equipment and software has been demonstrated.

The Commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 44 specifying which categories or classes of radio equipment are concerned by each of the requirements set out in points (a) to (i) of the first subparagraph of this paragraph.

1. The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the Commission subject to the conditions laid down in this Article.

2. The power to adopt delegated acts referred to in the second subparagraph of Articles 3(3), 4(2) and 5(2) shall be conferred on the Commission for a period of five years from 11 June 2014. The Commission shall draw up a report in respect of the delegation of power not later than nine months before the end of the five-year period. The delegation of power shall be tacitly extended for periods of an identical duration, unless the European Parliament or the Council opposes such extension not later than three months before the end of each period.

3. The delegation of power referred to in the second subparagraph of Articles 3(3), 4(2) and 5(2) may be revoked at any time by the European Parliament or by the Council. A decision to revoke shall put an end to the delegation of the power specified in that decision. It shall take effect the day following the publication of the decision in the Official Journal of the European Union or at a later date specified therein. It shall not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force.

4. As soon as it adopts a delegated act, the Commission shall notify it simultaneously to the European Parliament and to the Council.

A delegated act adopted pursuant to the second subparagraph of Articles 3(3), 4(2) and 5(2) shall enter into force only if no objection has been expressed either by the European Parliament or the Council within a period of two months of notification of that act to the European Parliament and the Council or if, before the expiry of that period, the European Parliament and the Council have both informed the Commission that they will not object. That period shall be extended by two months at the initiative of the European Parliament or of the Council.

[EN] Article 5 — By-products
  Act: Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives (Text with EEA relevance)
  Location: CHAPTER I SUBJECT MATTER, SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS
By-products

1. A substance or object, resulting from a production process, the primary aim of which is not the production of that item, may be regarded as not being waste referred to in point (1) of Article 3 but as being a by-product only if the following conditions are met:

(a)
further use of the substance or object is certain;

(b)
the substance or object can be used directly without any further processing other than normal industrial practice;

(c)
the substance or object is produced as an integral part of a production process; and

(d)
further use is lawful, i.e. the substance or object fulfils all relevant product, environmental and health protection requirements for the specific use and will not lead to overall adverse environmental or human health impacts.

2. On the basis of the conditions laid down in paragraph 1, measures may be adopted to determine the criteria to be met for specific substances or objects to be regarded as a by-product and not as waste referred to in point (1) of Article 3. Those measures, designed to amend non-essential elements of this Directive by supplementing it, shall be adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure with scrutiny referred to in Article 39(2).

[EN] Article 3 — Definitions
  Act: Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives (Text with EEA relevance)
  Location: CHAPTER I SUBJECT MATTER, SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS
Definitions

For the purposes of this Directive, the following definitions shall apply:

1.
‘waste’ means any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard;

2.
‘hazardous waste’ means waste which displays one or more of the hazardous properties listed in Annex III;

3.
‘waste oils’ means any mineral or synthetic lubrication or industrial oils which have become unfit for the use for which they were originally intended, such as used combustion engine oils and gearbox oils, lubricating oils, oils for turbines and hydraulic oils;

4.
‘bio-waste’ means biodegradable garden and park waste, food and kitchen waste from households, restaurants, caterers and retail premises and comparable waste from food processing plants;

5.
‘waste producer’ means anyone whose activities produce waste (original waste producer) or anyone who carries out pre-processing, mixing or other operations resulting in a change in the nature or composition of this waste;

6.
‘waste holder’ means the waste producer or the natural or legal person who is in possession of the waste;

7.
‘dealer’ means any undertaking which acts in the role of principal to purchase and subsequently sell waste, including such dealers who do not take physical possession of the waste;

8.
‘broker’ means any undertaking arranging the recovery or disposal of waste on behalf of others, including such brokers who do not take physical possession of the waste;

9.
‘waste management’ means the collection, transport, recovery and disposal of waste, including the supervision of such operations and the after-care of disposal sites, and including actions taken as a dealer or broker;

You select the question-generation mode for an EU legislative article: "fact_pattern" or "lookup".
Choose the mode that best fits the target article’s substantive content. Do not generate questions
or answers.

INPUT STRUCTURE
The input contains four marked blocks:
- "### TARGET ARTICLE": the article that questions must be about.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES": provisions cited from the same act.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS": provisions cited from other acts.
- "### REFERENCED ANNEXES": cited annexes.

References provide context or complete the target’s rule; they must not become the subject of the
questions.

Article blocks contain a language tag, article number and title, an "Act:" line identifying the
instrument and its subject matter, and sometimes a "Location:" within the act. Other-act references
and annexes have a "Cite as:" key identifying the provision. Empty blocks are marked.
Different-language versions represent the same provision.

Use metadata to understand the legal regime, but choose based on the target article’s text.

AVAILABLE MODES

FACT_PATTERN — The practitioner knows the situation, not the governing instrument.
Questions describe a concrete case involving a private party or a national authority handling a
file. The situation includes at least two legally relevant particulars, such as the actor, activity,
product, omission, quantity, place, or time. These instantiate conditions the article explicitly
addresses, without giving away the legal consequence.

Typical information needs: whether the case is covered, permitted, prohibited, or eligible; what the
actor must do; what deadline, amount, or consequence applies. Questions do not name the governing
instrument.

LOOKUP — The practitioner knows the regime and wants one point of law.
Questions directly request a definition, scope rule, obligation, condition, deadline, threshold,
reporting requirement, consequence, competent body, or procedure. They identify the regime through a
specific actor, product, activity, or legal term, without requiring a concrete client situation.

Each question has two otherwise identical renderings: one without an instrument identifier and one
with the target instrument’s official identifier.

SELECTION
Choose fact_pattern when meaningful case particulars naturally connect a situation to the target’s
legal treatment. Choose lookup when a direct request for a legal point is more natural and adding a
case would mainly decorate the question.

Both modes can cover the same legal topics; select by the question framing the article supports, not
simply by the presence of a definition, number, or deadline.

Return "skip" when neither mode is suitable, including when the target contains only boilerplate
such as transposition, entry into force, or generic institutional review clauses.

OUTPUT
Return valid JSON only:
{"mode": "<fact_pattern|lookup|skip>",
 "reason": "<one short sentence explaining the fit to this article>"}

- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES": provisions cited from the same act.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS": provisions cited from other acts.

References provide context or complete the target’s rule; they must not become the subject of the
questions.

Article blocks contain a language tag, article number and title, an "Act:" line identifying the
instrument and its subject matter, and sometimes a "Location:" within the act. Other-act references
and annexes have a "Cite as:" key identifying the provision. Empty blocks are marked.
Different-language versions represent the same provision.

Use metadata to understand the legal regime, but choose based on the target article’s text.

AVAILABLE MODES

FACT_PATTERN — The practitioner knows the situation, not the governing instrument.
Questions describe a concrete case involving a private party or a national authority handling a
file. The situation includes at least two legally relevant particulars, such as the actor, activity,
product, omission, quantity, place, or time. These instantiate conditions the article explicitly
addresses, without giving away the legal consequence.

Typical information needs: whether the case is covered, permitted, prohibited, or eligible; what the
actor must do; what deadline, amount, or consequence applies. Questions do not name the governing
instrument.

LOOKUP — The practitioner knows the regime and wants one point of law.
Questions directly request a definition, scope rule, obligation, condition, deadline, threshold,
reporting requirement, consequence, competent body, or procedure. They identify the regime through a
specific actor, product, activity, or legal term, without requiring a concrete client situation.

Each question has two otherwise identical renderings: one without an instrument identifier and one
with the target instrument’s official identifier.

SELECTION
Choose fact_pattern when meaningful case particulars naturally connect a situation to the target’s
legal treatment. Choose lookup when a direct request for a legal point is more natural and adding a
case would mainly decorate the question.

Both modes can cover the same legal topics; select by the question framing the article supports, not
simply by the presence of a definition, number, or deadline.

Return "skip" when neither mode is suitable, including when the target contains only boilerplate
such as transposition, entry into force, or generic institutional review clauses.

messages.content:
You select the question-generation mode for an EU legislative article: "fact_pattern" or "lookup".
Choose the mode that best fits the target article’s substantive content. Do not generate questions
or answers.

INPUT STRUCTURE
The input contains four marked blocks:
- "### TARGET ARTICLE": the article that questions must be about.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES": provisions cited from the same act.
- "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS": provisions cited from other acts.
- "### REFERENCED ANNEXES": cited annexes.

References provide context or complete the target’s rule; they must not become the subject of the
questions.

Article blocks contain a language tag, article number and title, an "Act:" line identifying the
instrument and its subject matter, and sometimes a "Location:" within the act. Other-act references
and annexes have a "Cite as:" key identifying the provision. Empty blocks are marked.
Different-language versions represent the same provision.

Use metadata to understand the legal regime, but choose based on the target article’s text.

AVAILABLE MODES

FACT_PATTERN — The practitioner knows the situation, not the governing instrument.
Questions describe a concrete case involving a private party or a national authority handling a
file. The situation includes at least two legally relevant particulars, such as the actor, activity,
product, omission, quantity, place, or time. These instantiate conditions the article explicitly
addresses, without giving away the legal consequence.

Typical information needs: whether the case is covered, permitted, prohibited, or eligible; what the
actor must do; what deadline, amount, or consequence applies. Questions do not name the governing
instrument.

LOOKUP — The practitioner knows the regime and wants one point of law.
Questions directly request a definition, scope rule, obligation, condition, deadline, threshold,
reporting requirement, consequence, competent body, or procedure. They identify the regime through a
specific actor, product, activity, or legal term, without requiring a concrete client situation.

Each question has two otherwise identical renderings: one without an instrument identifier and one
with the target instrument’s official identifier.

SELECTION
Choose fact_pattern when meaningful case particulars naturally connect a situation to the target’s
legal treatment. Choose lookup when a direct request for a legal point is more natural and adding a
case would mainly decorate the question.

Both modes can cover the same legal topics; select by the question framing the article supports, not
simply by the presence of a definition, number, or deadline.

Return "skip" when neither mode is suitable, including when the target contains only boilerplate
such as transposition, entry into force, or generic institutional review clauses.

OUTPUT
Return valid JSON only:
{"mode": "<fact_pattern|lookup|skip>",
 "reason": "<one short sentence explaining the fit to this article>"}

1. Each year, a beneficiary of the support referred to in Article 67(2) shall submit an application for direct payments or a payment claim for the relevant area and animal-related rural development measures respectively indicating, where applicable:

(a)

As regards the area-related direct payment, each Member State shall determine the minimum size of agricultural parcels in respect of which an application may be made. However, the minimum size shall not exceed 0,3 ha.

messages.content:
You are an expert at creating legal and regulatory retrieval questions from EU legislation.
FACT-PATTERN MODE — THE PRACTITIONER HAS A SITUATION, NOT A CITATION. Write each question as a
  lawyer, compliance officer or regulatory analyst would put it to a legal research assistant when
  describing a client's concrete situation and asking how EU law treats it. They do not name — and
  may not know — the instrument that governs it; the retriever must match the situation to the
  governing rule.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English whatever the source language. In
  the ANSWER, reproduce numbers, dates, durations, amounts, percentages and official identifiers
  exactly as the source states them ("100 000 EUR", not "€100,000"; "90 days", never "three
  months"). Use official English names of institutions and instruments, not literal translations.
  Identifiers ("Directive (EU) 2019/904", "Article 5(2)") may appear in an answer when the source
  states them; they never appear in a question.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Four marked blocks. "### TARGET ARTICLE" is the one article you write questions ABOUT. "###
  REFERENCED ARTICLES" (same act), "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS" and "### REFERENCED
  ANNEXES" hold provisions the target cites, supplied only so an answer can be COMPLETE — never as
  the subject of a question. Blocks from other acts and all annexes carry an "Act:" line and a "Cite
  as:" key; an empty block says so.
Each article block opens with metadata, then the text:
    [EN] Article 25 — Non-compliance by the responsible person
      Act: Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on cosmetic products (recast)
      Location: CHAPTER VIII NON-COMPLIANCE, SAFEGUARD CLAUSE
The Act line's opening words are the official identifier; the rest is the SUBJECT MATTER, your main
  source for the regime the situation must belong to. Metadata is context, not content: never take
  an answer from it and never ask about it. No question contains an identifier of any act, a CELEX
  number, a "Cite as" key, an article, paragraph or annex number, or deictic wording ("under this
  Regulation", "the measures set out herein") — the asker has not seen the document.
THE SITUATION — the defining rules of this mode:
1. PARTICULARS. The question describes a concrete case with at least TWO particulars that
  instantiate the CONDITIONS the target rule turns on — who (the actor as the law characterises it,
  in ordinary words: "a Finnish publisher", "a water utility running a design contest", "a paying
  agency in an outermost region"), what (the product, activity, transaction or omission), and, where
  the rule turns on it, how much / when / where. Report them in "particulars".
2. PROTAGONIST. A private party, or a national authority acting on a file (a paying agency, a
  competent authority handling an application, a customs office). Never the Commission, an EU agency
  or official, or a Member State as legislator — they are not clients, and the clauses addressed to
  them are institutional boilerplate.
3. INSIDE THE CASE. Place every particular where the article decides it: a quantity under the
  ceiling when the rule exempts what is under the ceiling; the Member State the article names; the
  omission the article makes a condition. Then the article's own words decide the case and no
  inference is needed. Never build a case whose outcome needs weighing, negation or reasoning the
  article does not state.
4. CONDITIONS, NEVER THE CONSEQUENCE. The situation says what the actor is and what it did or failed
  to do; it never says what the rule requires — for how long, to whom, in which form, at what rate.
  "A generation undertaking with one 250 MW plant is asked to keep its hourly data at the disposal
  of the national regulatory authority, the national competition authority and the Commission. Is it
  covered by the five-year storage duty?" hands the answer to the asker. Ask instead: "A generation
  undertaking's only plant has an installed capacity of 250 MW. For how long must it keep the
  plant's hourly generation data available to the regulators?" Test: delete the answer span from the
  article — if the situation could not have been written from what remains, it contains the answer.
5. PARTIAL FACTS, PLAIN WORDS, EXACT TERMS. A client presents two or three facts, never the
  article's full enumeration: when the article lists five products or four conditions, the situation
  names one or two ("plastic plates and straws", not all five items). Describe facts in plain
  business language, at a distance from the article's wording ("800 kg in one shipment" for
  "quantities not exceeding, per transaction, one tonne"; "criteria that were not in the contest
  notice" for "solely on the basis of the criteria indicated in the contest notice"). Keep terms of
  art, institution and programme names exactly — "producers" is not "manufacturers", "placing on the
  market" is not "selling", "taxable person" is not "business", "qualifying holding" has no synonym;
  a substituted term changes the rule. Legal text is sensitive to exact words: when unsure whether a
  word is load-bearing, keep it.
6. VOICE AND ASK. Third person, a practitioner describing a case — never "my landlord", "discuss
  whether", "what does the regulation say about", or a bare slot ("what must be taken into account
  when ..."). One ask per question: is it permitted / required / covered; what must the actor do;
  what rate, threshold or time limit applies; what is the consequence; which body decides. Yes/no is
  the default; the answer is always the span that decides the question, never "yes" or "no".
THE SIBLING TEST: EU legislation repeats provisions across sister acts, so the particulars must fix
  the regime. "An asset manager" fits UCITS, AIFMD and MiFID; "a UCITS management company" fits one.
  "A public buyer holding a design contest" fits the classic and utilities procurement directives;
  "a water utility" fits one. "A company importing goods subject to anti-dumping duty" fits every
  anti-dumping regulation; "wire rod from China" fits one, and the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy
  basic regulations share identical procedural articles, so say which proceeding it is. "A paying
  agency selecting farms for on-the-spot checks" fits the general CAP control rules; "in an
  outermost region" fits the outermost-regions rules. Would this situation be governed just as well
  by a different act? Add the fixing particular, or discard.
THE ONE-ARTICLE TEST: the question must turn on what the TARGET article lays down — its obligation,
  prohibition, condition, deadline, threshold or procedure. A referenced article may only COMPLETE
  the answer: name the members of a list the target points to, define a term it uses, give a value
  it defers to. Before keeping a question ask: could a reader answer it completely from a referenced
  article alone, never having seen the target? If yes, it belongs to that article — discard. This is
  the commonest failure in this task; in a production run every multi-article question failed it. If
  the answer's substance lies behind a citation that was NOT supplied, discard.
GROUNDING: the answer is a contiguous span of the supplied text — the target article, or a supplied
  referenced article the target's citation led to — that governs the situation as described. No
  inference beyond following an explicit cross-reference, no outside knowledge. Invented particulars
  are allowed in the question, never in the answer, and a particular that instantiates a threshold
  must sit on the correct side of it.
BOILERPLATE — SKIP: transposition, application-date, entry-into-force, addressee, "binding in its
  entirety", repeal, committee-procedure and definitive-collection clauses; and institutional
  clauses — Commission review/report clauses, annual implementation reports of financing
  instruments, agency evaluation clauses, financial-interests and audit-access clauses (Commission,
  Court of Auditors, OLAF), exercise-of-the-delegation clauses, penalties clauses that only require
  "effective, proportionate and dissuasive" penalties, data-protection cross-references. No fact
  pattern instantiates them and they are identical across hundreds of acts. If the target article is
  only such text, return the skip; if it holds such a clause beside substantive rules, ask about the
  substantive rules.
WHAT TO ASK — "question_type", one of eight; when returning two or three questions, cover at least two categories:
  1. scope_or_applicability — covered, exempt, excluded; precedence over other instruments.
  2. obligation_or_prohibition — the conduct described is required, forbidden or permitted, and for
    whom.
  3. condition_or_prerequisite — a condition for an exemption, approval or authorisation is met by
    the facts; what must be in place first.
  4. deadline_or_duration — the article's own substantive time rule for the request, report,
    decision or practice described.
  5. amount_or_threshold — the rate, cap, ceiling or percentage that applies.
  6. monitoring_or_reporting — what must be reported or notified, to whom, how often.
  7. enforcement_or_consequence — what follows from the failure described: refusal, suspension,
    withdrawal, penalty, nullity.
  8. definition_actor_or_procedure — whether the thing described counts as the defined term; which
    body decides; which procedure applies.
Purpose or rationale only when the text states it explicitly and completely.
DECLARING INVOLVED ARTICLES — "articles_involved" lists exactly the provisions a reader needs to
  produce the answer; it is graded, and an error here counts as a wrong answer:
- The target article is always listed. A referenced article is listed only if its content is part of
  the answer, never because the target mentions it.
- Bare numbers ("6", "7a") always mean articles of the target's own act. Articles of other acts and
  ALL annexes (the target act's included) are declared by the exact "Cite as" key of their block:
  ["4", "32004R0021:5"], ["4", "32019L0904:anx_1"].
EXAMPLES:
The following excerpts are simplified illustrations; their wording and article numbers are not
  authoritative legal quotations.
Example 1 — answer wholly inside the target article
### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 8 — Reporting obligations
  Act: Directive (EU) 2019/904 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the reduction of the impact of certain plastic products on the environment
"1. Producers shall report to the competent national authority, by 31 March each year, the quantities placed on the market. 2. Reports shall be submitted using the format referred to in Article 12."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES
[EN] Article 12 — Implementing powers
"The Commission shall adopt implementing acts establishing the format for the reports."
✓ {"question": "A producer placed 40 tonnes of single-use plastic cutlery on the Spanish market last year and has not yet reported the quantity to the Spanish authority. By when must it do so?", "answer": "by 31 March each year", "question_type": "deadline_or_duration", "particulars": ["producer", "40 tonnes of single-use plastic cutlery on the Spanish market last year", "has not yet reported the quantity"], "articles_involved": ["8"]}
  → The particulars fix the regime (single-use plastic) and the conduct; the article's own deadline
    answers. Article 12 is cited but contributed nothing, so it is not listed.
✗ "A company subject to the plastics rules wants to know its reporting deadline." → no actor,
  product or conduct: a slot in a costume.
✗ "A manufacturer that sold 40 tonnes of throwaway plastic forks last year …" → "sold" is not
  "placed on the market" and "manufacturer" is not "producer"; the question now describes a
  different rule.
✗ "A producer of single-use plastic cutlery is preparing its annual report. Which format must it
  use?" → the format sits behind an unsupplied implementing act. Discard.
Example 2 — answer completed by a referenced article
### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 4 — Placing on the market (Act: Directive (EU) 2019/904, as above)
"Member States shall prohibit the placing on the market of the single-use plastic articles listed in Article 3 from 3 July 2026."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES
[EN] Article 3 — Covered products
"This Directive applies to cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, straws and beverage stirrers made of plastic."
✓ {"question": "In August 2026, a retailer in Spain intends to keep placing plastic plates and straws on the market. Are they among the single-use plastic products the EU has banned?", "answer": "cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, straws and beverage stirrers made of plastic", "question_type": "scope_or_applicability", "particulars": ["August 2026", "retailer in Spain", "intends to keep placing plastic plates and straws on the market"], "articles_involved": ["3", "4"]}
  → The prohibition is the target's own rule; the list of products comes from Article 3, so both are
    declared. The situation names two of the five products, not the whole list: a question that
    copies the article's enumeration retrieves by string overlap and describes no real client.
    ONE-ARTICLE TEST: Article 3 lists products but never says they are banned — the ban is the
    target's fact.
✗ "A Spanish retailer sells plastic tableware. Which products does the single-use plastics directive
  cover?" → a question about Article 3; discard.
✗ {"question": "A Spanish retailer still has stock of the single-use plastic items covered by the EU ban. From what date can it no longer place them on the market?", "answer": "from 3 July 2026", "articles_involved": ["3", "4"]}
  → over-declared: the date is entirely in Article 4.
Example 3 — an article of ANOTHER act completes the answer
### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 2 — Payment of the aid
  Act: Commission Regulation (EC) No 796/2004 laying down detailed rules for the aid to sheep and goat holdings …
"The aid shall be paid only after the checks provided for in Article 5 of Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 have been carried out."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS
[EN] Article 5 — Checks   Act: Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 …   Cite as: 32004R0021:5
"Member States shall carry out on-the-spot checks covering at least 3 % of holdings each year."
✓ {"question": "A sheep farmer in Ireland has applied for this year's aid for sheep and goat holdings. Which checks must be completed before the aid can be paid?", "answer": "on-the-spot checks covering at least 3 % of holdings each year", "question_type": "condition_or_prerequisite", "particulars": ["sheep farmer in Ireland", "has applied for this year's aid for sheep and goat holdings"], "articles_involved": ["2", "32004R0021:5"]}
  → The payment condition is the target's rule; the other act only says what the checks are. The
    answer is a contiguous span of the referenced article. Both articles are declared, with the
    other act's article identified by its Cite as key; no identifier appears in the question.
✗ "An Irish paying agency is planning this year's livestock inspections. What share of sheep and
  goat holdings must it check on the spot?" → Article 5 of the other regulation answers this alone;
  it would retrieve that regulation. Discard.
Example 4 — real production questions repaired into fact patterns
(a) TARGET Article 1 of the Euratom regulation exempting small quantities of ores, source materials
  and special fissile materials from the Treaty's chapter on supplies: "(a) transfers within and
  imports into the Community of quantities not exceeding, per transaction a dosage of one tonne of
  uranium and thorium (or uranium or thorium), within a limit of five tonnes per year per user in
  respect of each of these materials; …"
✗ Generated: "How much uranium or thorium may be moved inside the Community, or brought into it, in
  a single deal before the exemption no longer applies?" → a paraphrased slot; no situation.
✓ {"question": "A company imports a single shipment of uranium ore containing 800 kg of uranium into the Union and expects to import about four tonnes of uranium in total this year. Is the shipment exempt from the Euratom Treaty's chapter on supplies?", "answer": "transfers within and imports into the Community of quantities not exceeding, per transaction a dosage of one tonne of uranium and thorium (or uranium or thorium), within a limit of five tonnes per year per user in respect of each of these materials", "question_type": "scope_or_applicability", "particulars": ["a single shipment of uranium ore", "800 kg of uranium", "about four tonnes of uranium in total this year"], "articles_involved": ["1"]}
  → Both thresholds instantiated on the inside, so the span decides without inference. With 1.2

(b) TARGET Article 98 of the utilities procurement directive — Decisions of the jury: "The jury

✗ Generated: "On what basis must the jury assess the submitted plans and projects?" → the same rule

✓ {"question": "A water utility is holding a design contest for a new treatment plant, and the jury wants to rank the entries partly on criteria that were not in the contest notice. ✗ Generated: "What share of the minimum number of aid applicants must Member States randomly select

✓ {"question": "A paying agency in an outermost region of the Union selects the aid applicants for on-the-spot checks purely on the basis of a risk analysis, with no random element. (d) TARGET Article 111 of the VAT Directive: "Subject to the conditions laid down in the second
  paragraph of Article 110, exemptions with deductibility of the VAT paid at the preceding stage may
  continue to be granted in the following cases: (a) by Finland in respect of the supply of
  newspapers and periodicals sold by subscription and …; (b) by Sweden …"
✗ Generated: "Which Finnish supplies may continue to benefit from VAT exemptions with
  deductibility?" → a slot, not a situation.
✓ {"question": "A Finnish publisher sells periodicals to readers by subscription. Are these supplies in one of the listed categories for continued VAT exemption with deduction of input VAT?", "answer": "by Finland in respect of the supply of newspapers and periodicals sold by subscription", "question_type": "scope_or_applicability", "particulars": ["Finnish publisher", "sells periodicals to readers by subscription"], "articles_involved": ["111"]}
  → "Finland" and "sold by subscription" instantiate the listed category's criteria. The question
    only identifies that category; it does not decide whether all conditions for exemption are met.
    A question turning on the Article 110 conditions would require that article to be supplied and
    ["111", "110"] to be declared; without it, discard.
Example 5 — real production questions to discard
✗ "A Commission official is asked to help two FIUs from different Member States coordinate a
  cross-border case and exchange information within the Union. May the Commission lend that
  assistance?" → the protagonist is the Commission and the situation restates the rule's
  consequence; the clause has no private-party case. Skip it, or use another provision of the
  article.
✗ "A Member State has only started drafting emergency response plans after a radiological emergency
  scenario has already been identified … Does the law require those plans to be established in
  advance for the various types of emergencies identified by an assessment of potential emergency
  exposure situations?" → the question contains the rule verbatim, and a Member State as legislator
  is not a client. Discard.
✗ "A Spanish retailer sells plastic straws. Does Article 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/904 apply to it?"
  → identifier in the question. Discard.
SELF-CHECK for each question before finalizing:
1. Situation with two or more particulars that instantiate the rule's CONDITIONS, all inside the
  case the article decides, reported in "particulars"; protagonist a private party or an authority
  on a file.
2. The situation states no consequence of the rule — delete the answer span from the article: could
  the situation still have been written?
3. SIBLING TEST: would a different act govern this situation just as well? Add the fixing particular
  or discard.
4. ONE-ARTICLE TEST: answerable from a referenced article alone? Discard. Answer's substance behind
  an unsupplied citation? Discard.
5. Facts in plain words, partial not enumerated; terms of art, names, and answer figures exact; no
  identifiers, article numbers or deixis in the question.
6. Answer a contiguous span of the supplied text that decides the case as described;
  "articles_involved" exactly the provisions used, target included, other acts and annexes by "Cite
  as" key.
7. Not boilerplate; one ask; third-person practitioner voice; the questions cover different facts
  and, when returning two or three questions, at least two categories.
OUTPUT (valid JSON only, no markdown): up to three entries, fewer if fewer pass every test:
[

- particulars: the two or more concrete facts of the situation, as short phrases, in the order they

  answer from it and never ask about it.
IDENTIFIERS AND DEIXIS: the base "question" contains no identifier of any act, no CELEX number, no
  "Cite as" key, no article, paragraph or annex number. "question_cited" contains the TARGET act's
  identifier only — never another act's, which would retrieve that act. Another act's identifier may
  appear inside an answer span when the source states it. No question uses deictic wording ("under
  this Regulation", "the annex hereto", "according to the text") or refers to article numbers as if
  visible: the asker has not seen the document. Bad: "What does Article 6 require in the case
  covered by Article 9?" → Good: "When is processing of health data lawful without consent?"
THE ANCHOR RULE — the defining rule of this mode:
Every question, in both renderings, carries at least one REGIME ANCHOR — a phrase that fixes which
  body of EU law is meant when no identifier is present:
  (a) the regulated actor as the law names it — "UCITS management company", "trade repository",
    "notified body for medical devices", "importer of herbal products for smoking";
  (b) the regulated product, activity or measure — "anti-dumping duty on aluminium foil in rolls
    from China", "cross-border VAT refund", "design contest run by a utilities-sector contracting
    entity", "export refunds for cheese";
  (c) a term of art that exists only in this regime — "qualifying holding", "undertaking-specific
    parameters", "active food contact materials", "take back request".
Generic actors are never anchors, because each appears in hundreds of acts: "Member States", "the
  Commission", "the competent authority", "the manufacturer", "the applicant", "the operator", "the
  jury", "the advisory body", "the compliance officer". Take the anchor from the subject-matter
  words of the Act line and the article text, and report it in "anchor" exactly as it appears in the
  base question.
THE SIBLING TEST: EU legislation repeats provisions across sister acts — near-identical
  authorisation, qualifying-holding and compliance-function rules across UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID, CRD
  and Solvency II; identical jury and design-contest rules in the 2014 procurement directives; the
  same "all other companies" clause in every anti-dumping regulation, and identical procedural
  articles in the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy basic regulations; the same 20–25 % random-sampling
  rule across the CAP control regulations; the same transposition clause in every directive. Before
  keeping a question ask: would it, word for word, be an equally sensible question about a DIFFERENT
  act? If yes, the anchor is missing — add it or discard. A question that only its identifier could
  disambiguate has no base rendering and fails.
THE COLLEAGUE TEST: read the question as a colleague who has not seen the article. Every "the X"
  must resolve from the question alone. "What must the advisory body monitor regarding the inventory
  of assets?" — which advisory body, what inventory? "What must Member States send the Commission
  about the material approved?" — what material, approved under what? These are
  reading-comprehension questions written by someone looking at the text. Name the actor and the
  regime, or turn the question into a yes/no question about the rule.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST: the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already
  contain. Two ways to fail it. Restatement — the answer repeats the question's words or the pointer
  it was built from: "in relation to matters to which it applies"; "a list of material approved" in
  reply to "what must they send about the material approved". Answer written into the question — the
  number, date, list or decision that constitutes the answer already appears in it: "Is the maritime
  accident investigation regime excluded for fishing vessels with a length of less than 15 metres?"
  contains its own answer; ask "Below what length are fishing vessels excluded from the maritime
  accident investigation regime?" (answer "15 metres"). Test: delete the answer span from the
  article — if the question could not have been written from what remains, it contains the answer.
  Write from the rule's conditions, never from its consequence, and ask about the substance: what
  the rule requires, permits or forbids, in which respects, for whom, by when.
PARAPHRASE WITHOUT DRIFT: rewrite the article's scaffolding in your own words — do not lift
  descriptive phrases, multi-word modifiers or sentence fragments, and do not reproduce an
  enumeration the article gives; copy terms of art, names of institutions and programmes, figures
  and dates exactly. "Annual deadline" may stand for "by 31 March each year", but "distribution
  numbers" may not stand for "quantities placed on the market": placing on the market is a term of
  art, and a substituted term changes the rule. The question may use practitioner vocabulary the
  text does not contain (a conventional regime name, an ordinary description of the actor); the
  answer may not. Legal text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is
  load-bearing, keep it.
BOILERPLATE — SKIP: transposition, application-date, entry-into-force, addressee, "binding in its
  entirety", repeal, committee-procedure and definitive-collection clauses; and institutional
  clauses — Commission review/report clauses ("accompanied, if necessary, by appropriate proposals
  or recommendations"), annual implementation reports of financing instruments, agency evaluation
  clauses ("every five years thereafter"), financial-interests and audit-access clauses (Commission,
  Court of Auditors, OLAF), exercise-of-the-delegation clauses, penalties clauses that only require
  "effective, proportionate and dissuasive" penalties, data-protection cross-references. All are
  identical across hundreds of acts and fail the sibling test by construction. If the target article
  is only such text, return the skip; if it holds such a clause beside substantive rules, ask about
  the substantive rules.
TWO RENDERINGS OF EACH QUESTION:
- "question": regime-anchored, identifier-free.
- "question_cited": the same words with the TARGET act's identifier inserted where a practitioner
  would put it ("Under Directive 2009/65/EC, …", "… under Commission Regulation (EU) No
  1300/2014?"). Copy the identifier from the opening words of the Act line — act type and number,
  retaining any Commission or Council qualifier that forms part of the identifier, but omitting
  the full enacting-institution formula, date and subject-matter title. Change nothing but the insertion: the anchor stays. "How
  often must the Commission report on the implementation of assistance under the Instrument for
  Stability?" must not become "Under Regulation (EC) No 1717/2006, how often must the Commission
  report on the implementation of the assistance?"
- "instrument_short_name": the conventional short name practitioners use for the TARGET act, if and
  only if one is in established use — "Mortgage Credit Directive", "UCITS Directive", "VAT
  Directive", "Tobacco Products Directive", "Utilities Directive", "EMIR", "Service Regulation".
  Otherwise null. Most implementing, delegated and amending acts and all anti-dumping regulations
  have none: never invent one, and never build one from the year and the title ("the 2014 EU
  directive on credit agreements for consumers relating to residential immovable property" is not a
  name anyone uses).
THE ONE-ARTICLE TEST: the question must turn on what the TARGET article lays down — its obligation,
  prohibition, condition, deadline, threshold or procedure. A referenced article may only COMPLETE
  the answer: name the members of a list the target points to, define a term it uses, give a value
  it defers to. Before keeping a question ask: could a reader answer it completely from a referenced
  article alone, never having seen the target? If yes, it belongs to that article — discard. This is
  the commonest failure in this task; in a production run every multi-article question failed it. If
  the answer's substance lies behind a citation that was NOT supplied, discard.
GROUNDING: the answer is the shortest contiguous span of the supplied text — the target article, or
  the target combined with a supplied referenced article — that fully answers the question; for a
  yes/no question, the span that decides it, never "yes" or "no". No inference beyond following an
  explicit cross-reference, no outside knowledge.
DECLARING INVOLVED ARTICLES — "articles_involved" lists exactly the provisions a reader needs to
  produce the answer; it is graded, and an error here counts as a wrong answer:
- The target article is always listed. A referenced article is listed only if its content is part of
  the answer, never because the target mentions it.
- Bare numbers ("6", "7a") always mean articles of the target's own act. Articles of other acts and
  ALL annexes (the target act's included) are declared by the exact "Cite as" key of their block:
  ["4", "32004R0021:5"], ["4", "32019L0904:anx_1"].
WHAT TO ASK — eight categories ("question_type"), each with the shapes practitioners use for it; the
  questions must cover at least two:
  1. scope_or_applicability — "Does [regime] apply to [actor / product / situation]?", "Is [X]
    excluded from [regime]?", "Which [products / entities] are covered by [regime]?"; includes
    precedence over other instruments.
  2. obligation_or_prohibition — "Does [actor] have to [X] under [regime]?", "May [actor] [do X]?",
    "What must [actor] do when [trigger]?"
  3. condition_or_prerequisite — "Under what conditions may [actor] [X]?", "What must be in place
    before [authority] grants [X]?"
  4. deadline_or_duration — "What is the time limit for [X] under [regime]?", "By when must [actor]
    [X]?" — the article's own substantive time rule; transposition and entry-into-force dates are
    boilerplate.
  5. amount_or_threshold — "What is the [rate / cap / threshold] for [X] under [regime]?", "Below
    what [quantity] does [rule] apply?"
  6. monitoring_or_reporting — "How often must [actor] report [X] to [recipient]?", "Whom must
    [actor] notify of [X]?"
  7. enforcement_or_consequence — "What happens if [actor] fails to [X]?", "May [authority] refuse /
    suspend / withdraw [X] when [Y]?"
  8. definition_actor_or_procedure — "What counts as [term] under [regime]?", "Which body [decides /
    monitors / approves] [X]?", "What is the procedure for [X]?"
Yes/no questions are welcome; they are the most common practitioner form. Every question asks for
  exactly ONE piece of information and carries a regime anchor; a bare slot ("What must be taken
  into account when …?", "What factors deserve special consideration …?") is not a question. Purpose
  or rationale only when the text states it explicitly and completely.

Conduct of Member States with regard to a bilateral investment agreement with a third country

Where a bilateral investment agreement falls within the scope of this Regulation, the Member State concerned shall:

(a)
inform the Commission without undue delay of all meetings which will take place under the provisions of the agreement. The Commission shall be provided with the agenda and all relevant information permitting an understanding of the topics to be discussed at those meetings. (b)
inform the Commission without undue delay of any representations made to it that a particular measure is inconsistent with the agreement. The Member State shall also immediately inform the Commission of any request for dispute settlement lodged under the auspices of the bilateral investment agreement as soon as the Member State becomes aware of such a request. The Member State and the Commission shall fully cooperate and take all necessary measures to ensure an effective defence which may include, where appropriate, the participation in the procedure by the Commission;

(c)
seek the agreement of the Commission before activating any relevant mechanisms for dispute settlement against a third country included in the bilateral investment agreement and shall, where requested by the Commission, activate such mechanisms. Those mechanisms shall include consultations with the other party to a bilateral investment agreement and dispute settlement where provided for in the agreement. The Member State and the Commission shall fully cooperate in the conduct of procedures within the relevant mechanisms, which may include, where appropriate, the participation in the relevant procedures by the Commission.

FACT-PATTERN MODE — THE PRACTITIONER HAS A SITUATION, NOT A CITATION. Write each question as a
  lawyer, compliance officer or regulatory analyst would put it to a legal research assistant when
  describing a client's concrete situation and asking how EU law treats it. They do not name — and
  may not know — the instrument that governs it; the retriever must match the situation to the
  governing rule.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English whatever the source language. In
  the ANSWER, reproduce numbers, dates, durations, amounts, percentages and official identifiers
  exactly as the source states them ("100 000 EUR", not "€100,000"; "90 days", never "three
  months"). Use official English names of institutions and instruments, not literal translations.
  Identifiers ("Directive (EU) 2019/904", "Article 5(2)") may appear in an answer when the source
  states them; they never appear in a question.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Four marked blocks. "### TARGET ARTICLE" is the one article you write questions ABOUT. "###
  REFERENCED ARTICLES" (same act), "### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS" and "### REFERENCED
  ANNEXES" hold provisions the target cites, supplied only so an answer can be COMPLETE — never as
  the subject of a question. Blocks from other acts and all annexes carry an "Act:" line and a "Cite
  as:" key; an empty block says so.
Each article block opens with metadata, then the text:

      Act: Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on cosmetic products (recast)
      Location: CHAPTER VIII NON-COMPLIANCE, SAFEGUARD CLAUSE
The Act line's opening words are the official identifier; the rest is the SUBJECT MATTER, your main
  source for the regime the situation must belong to. Metadata is context, not content: never take
  an answer from it and never ask about it. No question contains an identifier of any act, a CELEX
  number, a "Cite as" key, an article, paragraph or annex number, or deictic wording ("under this
  Regulation", "the measures set out herein") — the asker has not seen the document.
THE SITUATION — the defining rules of this mode:
1. PARTICULARS. The question describes a concrete case with at least TWO particulars that
  instantiate the CONDITIONS the target rule turns on — who (the actor as the law characterises it,
  in ordinary words: "a Finnish publisher", "a water utility running a design contest", "a paying
  agency in an outermost region"), what (the product, activity, transaction or omission), and, where
  the rule turns on it, how much / when / where. Report them in "particulars".
2. PROTAGONIST. A private party, or a national authority acting on a file (a paying agency, a
  competent authority handling an application, a customs office). Never the Commission, an EU agency
  or official, or a Member State as legislator — they are not clients, and the clauses addressed to
  them are institutional boilerplate.
3. INSIDE THE CASE. Place every particular where the article decides it: a quantity under the
  ceiling when the rule exempts what is under the ceiling; the Member State the article names; the
  omission the article makes a condition. Then the article's own words decide the case and no
  inference is needed. Never build a case whose outcome needs weighing, negation or reasoning the
  article does not state.
4. CONDITIONS, NEVER THE CONSEQUENCE. The situation says what the actor is and what it did or failed
  to do; it never says what the rule requires — for how long, to whom, in which form, at what rate.
  "A generation undertaking with one 250 MW plant is asked to keep its hourly data at the disposal
  of the national regulatory authority, the national competition authority and the Commission. Is it
  covered by the five-year storage duty?" hands the answer to the asker. Ask instead: "A generation
  undertaking's only plant has an installed capacity of 250 MW. For how long must it keep the
  plant's hourly generation data available to the regulators?" Test: delete the answer span from the
  article — if the situation could not have been written from what remains, it contains the answer.

  article's full enumeration: when the article lists five products or four conditions, the situation
  names one or two ("plastic plates and straws", not all five items). Describe facts in plain
  business language, at a distance from the article's wording ("800 kg in one shipment" for
  "quantities not exceeding, per transaction, one tonne"; "criteria that were not in the contest
  notice" for "solely on the basis of the criteria indicated in the contest notice"). Keep terms of
  art, institution and programme names exactly — "producers" is not "manufacturers", "placing on the
  market" is not "selling", "taxable person" is not "business", "qualifying holding" has no synonym;
  a substituted term changes the rule. Legal text is sensitive to exact words: when unsure whether a
  word is load-bearing, keep it.

  whether", "what does the regulation say about", or a bare slot ("what must be taken into account
  when ..."). One ask per question: is it permitted / required / covered; what must the actor do;
  what rate, threshold or time limit applies; what is the consequence; which body decides. Yes/no is
  the default; the answer is always the span that decides the question, never "yes" or "no".

  the regime. "An asset manager" fits UCITS, AIFMD and MiFID; "a UCITS management company" fits one.
  "A public buyer holding a design contest" fits the classic and utilities procurement directives;
  "a water utility" fits one. "A company importing goods subject to anti-dumping duty" fits every
  anti-dumping regulation; "wire rod from China" fits one, and the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy
  basic regulations share identical procedural articles, so say which proceeding it is. "A paying
  agency selecting farms for on-the-spot checks" fits the general CAP control rules; "in an
  outermost region" fits the outermost-regions rules. Would this situation be governed just as well
  by a different act? Add the fixing particular, or discard.

  prohibition, condition, deadline, threshold or procedure. A referenced article may only COMPLETE
  the answer: name the members of a list the target points to, define a term it uses, give a value
  it defers to. Before keeping a question ask: could a reader answer it completely from a referenced
  article alone, never having seen the target? If yes, it belongs to that article — discard. This is
  the commonest failure in this task; in a production run every multi-article question failed it. If
  the answer's substance lies behind a citation that was NOT supplied, discard.

  referenced article the target's citation led to — that governs the situation as described. No
  inference beyond following an explicit cross-reference, no outside knowledge. Invented particulars
  are allowed in the question, never in the answer, and a particular that instantiates a threshold
  must sit on the correct side of it.

  entirety", repeal, committee-procedure and definitive-collection clauses; and institutional

  instruments, agency evaluation clauses, financial-interests and audit-access clauses (Commission,

Example 1 — answer wholly inside the target article
### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 8 — Reporting obligations
  Act: Directive (EU) 2019/904 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the reduction of the impact of certain plastic products on the environment
"1. Producers shall report to the competent national authority, by 31 March each year, the quantities placed on the market. 2. Reports shall be submitted using the format referred to in Article 12."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES
[EN] Article 12 — Implementing powers
"The Commission shall adopt implementing acts establishing the format for the reports."
✓ {"question": "A producer placed 40 tonnes of single-use plastic cutlery on the Spanish market last year and has not yet reported the quantity to the Spanish authority.   product or conduct: a slot in a costume.
✗ "A manufacturer that sold 40 tonnes of throwaway plastic forks last year …" → "sold" is not

✗ "A producer of single-use plastic cutlery is preparing its annual report. Which format must it

Example 2 — answer completed by a referenced article
### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 4 — Placing on the market (Act: Directive (EU) 2019/904, as above)
"Member States shall prohibit the placing on the market of the single-use plastic articles listed in Article 3 from 3 July 2026."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES
[EN] Article 3 — Covered products
"This Directive applies to cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, straws and beverage stirrers made of plastic."

    copies the article's enumeration retrieves by string overlap and describes no real client.

✗ "A Spanish retailer sells plastic tableware. Which products does the single-use plastics directive

✗ {"question": "A Spanish retailer still has stock of the single-use plastic items covered by the EU ban. From what date can it no longer place them on the market?", "answer": "from 3 July 2026", "articles_involved": ["3", "4"]}
  → over-declared: the date is entirely in Article 4.

### TARGET ARTICLE
[EN] Article 2 — Payment of the aid
  Act: Commission Regulation (EC) No 796/2004 laying down detailed rules for the aid to sheep and goat holdings …
"The aid shall be paid only after the checks provided for in Article 5 of Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 have been carried out."
### REFERENCED ARTICLES FROM OTHER ACTS
[EN] Article 5 — Checks   Act: Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 …   Cite as: 32004R0021:5
"Member States shall carry out on-the-spot checks covering at least 3 % of holdings each year."
✓ {"question": "A sheep farmer in Ireland has applied for this year's aid for sheep and goat holdings.   → The payment condition is the target's rule; the other act only says what the checks are. The
    answer is a contiguous span of the referenced article. Both articles are declared, with the
    other act's article identified by its Cite as key; no identifier appears in the question.
✗ "An Irish paying agency is planning this year's livestock inspections. What share of sheep and
  goat holdings must it check on the spot?" → Article 5 of the other regulation answers this alone;
  it would retrieve that regulation. Discard.

(a) TARGET Article 1 of the Euratom regulation exempting small quantities of ores, source materials
  and special fissile materials from the Treaty's chapter on supplies: "(a) transfers within and
  imports into the Community of quantities not exceeding, per transaction a dosage of one tonne of
  uranium and thorium (or uranium or thorium), within a limit of five tonnes per year per user in
  respect of each of these materials; …"
✗ Generated: "How much uranium or thorium may be moved inside the Community, or brought into it, in
  a single deal before the exemption no longer applies?" → a paraphrased slot; no situation.
✓ {"question": "A company imports a single shipment of uranium ore containing 800 kg of uranium into the Union and expects to import about four tonnes of uranium in total this year. Is the shipment exempt from the Euratom Treaty's chapter on supplies?", "answer": "transfers within and imports into the Community of quantities not exceeding, per transaction a dosage of one tonne of uranium and thorium (or uranium or thorium), within a limit of five tonnes per year per user in respect of each of these materials", "question_type": "scope_or_applicability", "particulars": ["a single shipment of uranium ore", "800 kg of uranium", "about four tonnes of uranium in total this year"], "articles_involved": ["1"]}

    tonnes in one shipment the outcome would be a verdict you derive, not a span — discard such a
    case.

  shall examine the plans and projects submitted by the candidates anonymously and solely on the
  basis of the criteria indicated in the contest notice."
✗ Generated: "On what basis must the jury assess the submitted plans and projects?" → the same rule
  stands in the classic procurement directive; "the jury" resolves nothing.
✓ {"question": "A water utility is holding a design contest for a new treatment plant, and the jury wants to rank the entries partly on criteria that were not in the contest notice. ✗ "A contracting authority holding a design contest wants to …" → fits the classic directive
  equally; "water utility" is what fixes the regime.

  provide the element of representativeness, Member States shall randomly select between 20 and 25 %
  of the minimum number of aid applicants to be subjected to on-the-spot checks."
✗ Generated: "What share of the minimum number of aid applicants must Member States randomly select
  to ensure representativeness?" → the same rule exists in the general CAP control regulation; no
